title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, and benchmarking suite
author: Jordan Reyes
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving-runtime documentation for the runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, and the day-to-day runbooks and team wiki pointers. It is intended as the single reference for engineers operating or evolving Redwood's inference runtime in hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals
- Describe the high-level and component-level runtime architecture and data/control planes.
- Capture kernel selection and scheduling policies that drive performance and cost tradeoffs.
- Provide reproducible profiling/playbook steps for common performance investigations.
- Document the standardized benchmarking suite and test harness used for model onboarding and release validation.
- Surface recent release notes and outstanding known issues.
- Provide actionable runbooks for oncall and SRE teams and link to the runtime team wiki.

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (team)
- Document author: Jordan Reyes
- Oncall rotation: eng-sre (see runbook below)
- Primary reviewers: Priya Kumar (Runtime), Ethan Li (SRE), Maya Chen (Performance)

High-level runtime architecture

Summary
The serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine with a control plane that orchestrates model versions, routing, and autoscaling. Key goals: low tail latency (p50/p95), high throughput, cost-efficient batch utilization, and predictable behavior across hosted/dedicated/private modes.

Core components
- Frontend Router: HTTP/gRPC ingress that handles rate limiting, authentication, route resolution, and initial request shaping.
- Request Router & Policy Engine: routes requests by policy (latency vs cost), enforces fallbacks to compatible model variants, and decides placement (local GPU, remote pool, cold-spot).
- Batcher & KV-cache layer: performs continuous batching with per-model and per-route batching policies. Prefix/KV caching reduces compute for repeated prefixes.
- Execution Engine: GPU kernels and operators with quantization-aware paths; manages KV cache, attention caching, memory allocation, and kernel selection.
- Worker Pool & Scheduler: manages GPU allocation, lifecycle, and kernel scheduling decisions (see Kernel Scheduling).
- Telemetry & Tracing: per-token cost/latency breakdown, GPU metrics, kernel-level traces, and end-to-end traces integrated into Redwood Console.

Service names (examples)
- router-api (ingress)
- policy-engine (routing + fallback)
- batcher (continuous batching)
- exec-worker (GPU execution process)
- runtime-orchestrator (autoscale + placement)
- telemetry-agent (metrics & traces)

SLOs and thresholds (production targets)
- p50 latency per token: 15ms
- p95 latency per request: 250ms for 2K context short-compute models
- error budget: 99.9% availability per region per month
- GPU utilization target: 60-75% for amortized cost efficiency (depends on workload)

Kernel scheduling and policy guide

Goals
- Maximize throughput while preserving latency SLOs.
- Prefer kernels that minimize memory footprint and provide low per-token latency for common sequence lengths.
- Favor quantized kernels for cost-sensitive routes if quality delta within configured thresholds.

Decision factors for kernel selection
- Model architecture: causal LM vs encoder-decoder calls for different attention implementations.
- Sequence length distribution: short-seq optimized kernels (faster small-batch) vs long-seq kernels (memory optimized).
- Batch size and concurrency: some kernels scale better with batch size; schedule accordingly.
- Hardware capability: Tensor cores, mixed-precision support, and specialized instructions (A100 vs H100 vs V100).
- Quantization profile: int8/4 kernels if model passes quality gates.

Scheduler algorithm (summary)
1. Request classification: classify requests by model, prompt length, and latency tier.
2. Candidate kernel selection: lookup per-model kernel preference table (model metadata).
3. Affinity and co-location check: place requests to workers with compatible cache/KV state or to warm workers to avoid cold-start overhead.
4. Batch formation: continuous batching with time cap (configurable default 5ms) and max batch size per worker.
5. Kernel dispatch: launch kernel variant selected with fallback on OOM/timeout to a safer kernel variant.
6. Telemetry report: emit kernel-level metrics and batch composition for runtime analysis.

Config table (examples)
| config_key | default | notes |
|-----------|---------|-------|
| batching.time_cap_ms | "5" | max wait time before dispatching a batch |
| batching.max_size | "64" | upper bound batch size per worker |
| kernel.fallback_timeout_ms | "250" | kernel hard timeout before fallback |
| scheduling.affinity_enabled | "true" | enable worker-state affinity |
| quantization.threshold_accuracy_drop | "0.01" | max allowed accuracy drop for quantized kernels |

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to run
- Degraded p95 latency or elevated tail latency.
- New model onboarding or kernel rollout.
- Regression alerts triggered by quality/perf monitoring.

Quick triage steps
1. Confirm the scope: identify affected routes/models, regions, and time window. Use Console traces and per-route latency dashboards.
2. Isolate traffic pattern changes: check traffic mix, average sequence length, and client-side retries.
3. Check worker-level metrics: GPU utilization, cuda-mem-alloc failures, CPU steal, and queue depths.
4. Enable debug sampling for traces if needed (10-100 requests/min).

Profiling commands and artifacts
- Capture kernel-level traces on a warm worker:
```
# run on worker node
sudo perf record -F 200 -a -g -- /opt/redwood/runtime/bin/exec-worker --trace-kernels --trace-output /tmp/kernel-trace.pb
```
- Collect GPU metrics: nvidia-smi dmon or DCGM exporter snapshot
- Use runtime profiler:
```
/opt/redwood/runtime/tools/runtime-profiler --model <model-name> --seq-len 128 --batch 8 --out /tmp/profile.json
```
- Upload artifacts to diagnostics storage: rwd diagnostics upload /tmp/*.pb /tmp/*.json --incident $INCIDENT_ID

Analysis checklist
- Batch formation: verify average batch size and batching.wait cap.
- Kernel selection: confirm kernel variant and hardware used.
- Memory behavior: check peak allocation and GC/spill events.
- Latency contributors: tokenization, pre/post-processing, kernel exec, serialization.

Benchmarking suite and model onboarding harness

Purpose
The benchmark suite provides reproducible micro- and macro-benchmarks for model performance, calibration of batching/quantization configs, and CI gates for runtime releases.

Components
- micro-bench: single-worker kernel-level latency and memory profiles (seq len sweep, batch sweep).
- load-sim: multi-worker throughput tests with realistic request distributions and jitter.
- quality-eval: prompt set evaluation harness to verify quantized/optimized models do not regress beyond thresholds.
- ci-gates: automated checks run in PRs and nightly pipelines.

Sample CI job YAML (simplified)
```
job: model-onboard-benchmark
steps:
  - checkout
  - setup-gpu
  - run: /opt/redwood/runtime/bench/run-micro-bench --model $MODEL --seq 128,512 --batches 1,8,32 --out results.json
  - run: /opt/redwood/runtime/bench/run-load-sim --profile load_profiles/common.json --duration 600 --out load.json
  - run: /opt/redwood/runtime/bench/quality-eval --eval-set evals/translation-1k.json --baseline $BASE --candidate $CAND --out quality.json
  - upload-artifact: results.json load.json quality.json
```

Release notes (recent highlights)
- 2026-02-10: Exec-worker v2.3.0: improved kernel selector for H100, reduced p95 by ~12% for short-seq traffic.
- 2026-01-05: Batcher v1.8: continuous batching time cap adaptive mode enabled by default.
- 2025-11-20: Quantization toolchain v0.9: added int4 simulated fallback and quality gates.

Known issues (open)
- K-1023: Occasionally exec-worker OOMs on long-sequence (>=64k tokens) requests when co-located with other heavy jobs (mitigation: limit co-location and set per-worker max-seq).
- K-1094: On H100 with driver version X.Y.Z, there is a transient 5-10ms spike in kernel launch latency under high concurrency (workaround: pin to driver X.Y.(Z-1) while we test).
- K-1142: Quantized int4 kernels show a 0.8-1.5% BLEU regression on specific translation prompts for model t-7b-merged; flagged under quality-eval and disabled by default for that model.

Runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook: High tail latency (p95 elevated)
1. Identify affected routes/models in Console and check per-route breakdown.
2. Check recent deploys: kernel changes, quantization rollout, or autoscale policy changes.
3. SSH to a warm exec-worker and run quick profiler: runtime-profiler --short-scan --out /tmp/quick.json
4. If batcher backlog > threshold (default 1000ms), scale up worker pool or reduce batching.time_cap_ms.
5. If OOM observed, set kernel.fallback to conservative variant and restart exec-worker.
6. Create incident and attach profiling artifacts; pager to eng-sre and runtime oncall.

Runbook: GPU OOMs on worker
1. Isolate the container and collect dmesg and nvidia logs.
2. Check model max-seq and per-worker sequence limits; apply temporary cap: rwdctl worker update --id <id> --max-seq 4096
3. Restart the exec-worker process with safe environment: systemctl restart exec-worker@node
4. If persistent, cordon node and schedule maintenance.

Appendix: example model metadata snippet
```
model: t-7b-merged
preferred_kernels:
  - name: causal_fused_attn_h100_fp16
    min_seq: 1
    max_seq: 1024
  - name: causal_attn_memopt_fp16
    min_seq: 1025
    max_seq: 4096
quant_profiles: ["int8_default", "int4_experimental"]
quality_gates:
  max_bleu_drop: 0.015
```

Maintenance cadence and suggestions
- Nightly CI: run core benchmarking suite against representative models (small, medium, large).
- Weekly: review p95 regressions and kernel-fallback events.
- Monthly: update kernel selector heuristics based on real traffic distributions and hardware fleet changes.

If you find gaps or have improvements, open a PR against this page or create an RFC in /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records and tag eng-serving-runtime.
